findings.description: The 'data' bucket sets no ACL and no public access block, and the comment states it is public; a public S3 bucket exposes all objects (including customer-master.xlsx) to anonymous readers on the internet.
No server_side_encryption_configuration block is defined, so objects containing customer master data are stored without enforced KMS/SSE encryption at rest.
No logging block is configured, so access to this bucket produces no audit trail, hindering detection and investigation of unauthorised access.
Versioning is not enabled, so objects can be overwritten or deleted irreversibly (including by an attacker or ransomware) with no recovery of prior versions.
A customer master spreadsheet is uploaded into the publicly accessible, unencrypted 'data' bucket, and the source file is committed to the repository, exposing sensitive customer data.
The financials bucket has no server_side_encryption_configuration, so financial data is stored without enforced encryption at rest.
No logging block is configured for the financials bucket, leaving no audit trail of object access.
Versioning is not enabled on the financials bucket, so deletions or overwrites of sensitive financial records are unrecoverable.
The operations bucket lacks server_side_encryption_configuration, storing data unencrypted at rest.
No logging block is configured for the operations bucket, so there is no audit trail of who accessed objects.
The data_science bucket has no server_side_encryption_configuration, so data science datasets are stored unencrypted at rest.
The logs bucket (like all buckets here) has no aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block, so account or bucket ACL/policy changes could expose stored access logs publicly.
